title: Privileged Access Management
summary: Privileged access management is the set of controls that govern accounts with elevated rights, such as domain administrators, root on Unix hosts, cloud owner roles, database administrators and the service accounts that automation uses. The tooling usually provides a credential vault, session brokering with recording, just in time elevation with approval, automated rotation or short lived credentials, and discovery of where privileged credentials are stored across scripts, configuration files and vendor support arrangements. The core risk is not only the compromise of one powerful account but the accumulation of standing access and unmanaged credentials that nobody can enumerate. Removing standing administrator rights, so that elevation is requested for a task and expires afterwards, shrinks the window in which a stolen session is useful. Detection complements the controls: changes to privileged group membership, unusual privileged session behaviour, service accounts authenticating from unexpected hosts, and logons from impossible locations are all high value signals. The common misunderstanding is treating the product as a password vault and nothing more, when the measurable improvement comes from eliminating standing access and making sessions visible. The other frequent mistake is granting permanent administrator rights out of convenience because the approval workflow is slow, which quietly returns the environment to where it started.

beginner.definition: Privileged access management controls the accounts that have extra power. A privileged account can change settings, install software or read almost everything. These controls store the passwords safely and hand them out only when needed. They also record what was done while the account was in use.
beginner.whyItMatters: If an attacker takes over one powerful account, they can often take over everything. Passwords shared inside a team or left in a script make that easier. Long lived passwords are rarely changed and rarely noticed when stolen. Managing these accounts limits the damage and gives you a record to investigate.
howItWorks: Find every powerful account, including the ones used by scripts and outside suppliers.
Store those passwords in a protected vault instead of notes, files or shared documents.
Give people normal accounts for daily work and let them request extra rights only when needed.
Approve each request, then remove the extra rights automatically when the task ends.
Record the session so you can see and review what was changed and by whom.
Change the passwords on a schedule and watch the logs for unusual use of these accounts.
beginner.example: Think of a hospital store cupboard for strong medicines. Nobody carries the key all day. A nurse signs for the key, opens the cupboard, takes what the patient needs, and returns the key. The store log shows who had the key and when. If something goes missing, the log tells the manager where to look.
takeaways: Remove standing administrator rights and grant them only for a task.
Discover the credentials hidden in scripts and supplier arrangements.
Record privileged sessions, because you cannot review what you cannot see.

objectives: Define privileged access management and list the account types it covers.
Explain why standing, always available administrator rights increase risk.
Describe how vaulting, session recording and just in time elevation work together.
Explain why service accounts and vendor access paths are frequently overlooked.
Identify log sources and events that indicate misuse of privileged accounts.
Describe how an approval workflow that is too slow undermines the control.
